help.intro: A short text of about 150 words about German bread: there are more than three thousand kinds, the bakers keep a register of them, and since 2014 German bread culture is on the national list of cultural heritage. The text also tells you how to buy bread in a bakery without embarrassment: what a Brötchen is, why it has a different name in each region, and what to say at the counter. The facts are real and were checked. You need what you have just learnt: quantities (ein Kilo, fünfhundert Gramm, ein Stück, eine Scheibe, ein halbes Brot) and the accusative after kaufen, möchten and nehmen (Ich nehme einen Laib, ein Brötchen, eine Brezel). Read for the gist first, then find one number or one word per question.
help.tips[0].title: Quantities at the bakery
help.tips[0].text: ein Kilo Brot, fünfhundert Gramm Vollkornbrot, ein halbes Brot (half a loaf), ein ganzes Brot, ein Stück Kuchen, eine Scheibe Brot (a slice), zwei Brötchen, ein Laib (a loaf). After a quantity the noun has no article: ein Kilo Brot, not ein Kilo das Brot. Prices: das Kilo kostet, das Stück kostet.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: I would like half a loaf and four rolls, please.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: The wholemeal bread costs three euros fifty a kilo.
help.tips[0].check.why: Scheibe = slice. Stück = piece (cake), Laib = whole loaf.
help.tips[1].title: Accusative after kaufen, nehmen, möchten
help.tips[1].text: What you buy is the direct object and takes the accusative: der Laib → Ich kaufe einen Laib. das Brötchen → Ich nehme ein Brötchen. die Brezel → Ich möchte eine Brezel. Only masculine changes: der/ein → den/einen. Feminine, neuter and plural look like the nominative.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: I will take a loaf of rye bread and a pretzel.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: Do you have the bread? No, I will buy it later.
help.tips[1].check.why: der Kuchen is masculine; in the accusative ein becomes einen.
help.remember[0]: ein Laib, ein halbes Brot, eine Scheibe, fünfhundert Gramm, ein Stück Kuchen: no article after a quantity.
help.remember[1]: Masculine accusative: Ich nehme einen Laib, den Kuchen.
help.exam: Short texts about food and shopping with quantities, prices and multiple-choice questions are a typical reading task at this level.
help.hook: More than three thousand kinds of bread, a register to keep track of them, and ten names for one roll. Read why bread is so serious in Germany.
help.vocab[0].example: In Deutschland gibt es mehr als dreitausend Brotsorten.
passageTranslation:
In Germany there are more than three thousand kinds of bread. That is a world record! The bakers have a bread register: every bread is listed there with its name and recipe. Since 2014 German bread culture is officially cultural heritage.

Why so many breads? Germany has a lot of rye and wheat, and every region has its own bread. In the north people eat dark bread, in the south pretzels and white bread. The most important bread is the mixed bread made from rye and wheat.

In the bakery you buy a whole loaf or half a loaf. A kilo of bread costs about three to five euros. Many people also buy rolls. A Brötchen is a small bread. But careful: the word is different in every region! In Berlin people say Schrippe, in Bavaria Semmel, in Hamburg Rundstück, in Swabia Weckle. All mean the same small bread.

Germans eat a lot of bread: about fifty kilos per person a year. In the morning they eat rolls with butter and jam. In the evening many families eat bread with cheese and cold meat. That is called Abendbrot, evening bread.
